crop.notes: Bottom cut mid-sentence in the Jack Looney paragraph; the article continues at the top of the next column. The Allen and Coburn portions are complete.

ocr.notes: A few word errors ('Pom' for 'palmy', 'og' for 'dizzy').

title.suggested: Gone to the Dogs: Allen and McCoole Fall on Hard Times

summary.suggested: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reprinted a Minneapolis Tribune piece on fighters ruined by defeat, saying Allen had lost the fortune he made and now barely made a living from a saloon on Market Street.

metadata.notes: Masthead: St. Louis Daily Globe-Democrat, Saturday Morning, December 6, 1884. Reprinted from the Minneapolis Tribune.

facts.fact: Allen was said to be running a 'rather dizzy concern' on Market Street, St. Louis, barely making a living, having lost the money he made in his prime
After the Coburn fight Allen was said to have fled to Birmingham, England, to escape going to the penitentiary
Coburn was said to have served a term in the Pennsylvania State Prison on account of his fight with Allen
About eighteen months after Mike McCoole's wedding, Allen beat him, after which McCoole lost his bar and ended up working cotton bales on the New Orleans levee

notes: Secondhand recollections by an unnamed Minneapolis fighter; the Coburn first name is not given in the article.
